title: Python Name Binding and Dynamic Typing
learningObjectives: Explain assignment as binding a name to an object.
Distinguish a variable name from the object it refers to.
Explain reassignment without assuming an object was modified.
Use type inspection to observe a name referring to different object types.

understand.concept: In Python, assignment binds a name to an object. A name does not permanently own a fixed type: it can later be rebound to an object of another type. This behaviour is commonly called dynamic typing. The object's type belongs to the object, while the name is a reference used to access it. Rebinding one name does not automatically mutate the old object or change other names that refer to it.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding name binding clarifies why assignment, mutation and copying are different operations. It helps learners reason about function arguments, collections and shared references later in the course.
understand.analogy: A variable name is like a label attached to a reference card. Moving the label to another object changes what the name refers to; it does not transform the original object.
understand.analogyLimit: The label analogy is simplified: Python's object model, reference counting and garbage collection are implementation details and should not be inferred from a physical label.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Assignment binds a name

An assignment such as `score = 10` evaluates the right-hand side and binds the name `score` to the resulting object. The equals sign is an assignment operator, not a declaration that permanently fixes the name's type.

## 2. Dynamic typing

A name can be rebound to an object of another type. For example, `value = 10` followed by `value = 'ten'` is valid Python. The integer object is not converted into a string; the name now refers to a different object.

## 3. Multiple names and one object

Assignment can bind more than one name to the same object. Whether later changes are visible through both names depends on whether the object is mutable and whether the operation mutates it or rebinds a name.

## 4. Inspect types

Use `type(value)` to inspect the current object's type. Use `isinstance(value, SomeType)` for compatibility checks. These functions inspect the object currently referenced by the name.

## 5. Keep code understandable

Although rebinding across types is permitted, use descriptive names and consistent roles in application code. Avoid reusing one name for unrelated kinds of values because it makes programs harder to understand.

examples.title: Rebind a name to another type
examples.explanation: The name first refers to an integer and is later rebound to a string. The object types are not changed in place.

examples.title: Two names refer to one immutable object
examples.explanation: Both names refer to the same string value. Strings are immutable, so operations produce new strings rather than changing this one.

examples.title: Rebinding one name does not rebind another
examples.code:
left = 25
right = left
left = 40
print(left)
print(right)
examples.explanation: The assignment to left changes only the binding of left. right continues to refer to the integer object 25.

examples.title: Inspect a current object
examples.explanation: Both checks inspect the list object currently referenced by data.

examples.title: Observe expression result types
examples.explanation: The original name count refers to an int, while true division produces a float assigned to ratio.

practise.guidedTask: Assign an integer to a name, inspect its type, then reassign the name to a string and inspect the type again. Explain why this is not an in-place conversion.
practise.independentTask: Create two names that initially refer to the same integer value. Reassign one name and print both. Then repeat with a mutable list and observe how assignment differs from mutation.
hints: Assignment binds a name to an object.
Python names are not permanently restricted to one type.
Reassignment is not the same as mutation.
Another name is not automatically rebound when one name changes.
Use type() and isinstance() to inspect the current object.
practise.challenge: Write a short demonstration that contrasts rebinding a name, mutating a list and creating a new list. Explain which names observe each change.

questions.prompt: What does a normal assignment statement do?
options: Binds a name to an object
Permanently declares a fixed variable type
questions.answer: Binds a name to an object
questions.explanation: Assignment evaluates the expression and binds the target name to the resulting object.

questions.prompt: What does dynamic typing mean in Python?
options: A name can refer to objects of different types over time
Every name must be declared with a fixed type
Python changes every object into a string
Types are checked only by the browser
questions.answer: A name can refer to objects of different types over time
questions.explanation: Python determines an object's type at runtime, and names can be rebound to different objects.

questions.prompt: After x = 5; y = x; x = 9, what is y?
questions.explanation: The assignment to x rebinds x only. y remains bound to the integer value 5.

questions.prompt: Does rebinding a name change the type of the old object?
questions.explanation: Rebinding changes which object the name refers to; it does not mutate the old object.

questions.prompt: Which function reports the type of the current object?
questions.explanation: type(value) returns the type of the object currently referenced by value.
